Use of words As Desired and As Required
As desired allows pilot preference in switch/control positioning.
As required indicates those actions which vary based on mission requirements or dedicated SOP instructions.

This section is furnished for familiarization use. It will normally be inserted between BEFORE ENTERING COCKPIT and COCKPIT INTERIOR CHECK. It may also be inserted in another part of the checklist, removed, parts removed, or discarded as desired.

A thorough cockpit interior preflight shall be accomplished prior to each flight. The design features of the aircraft greatly simplify this task, but do not alleviate the requirement. Switch positions designated AS DESIRED allow pilot preference in switch/control positioning. AS REQUIRED indicates those switches that will differ with mission requirements. If no specific requirement exists, pilot preference may be used. Normally, those avionics switches designated AS DESIRED or AS REQUIRED should be OFF for start.

items.text: Normal engine start procedure does not use external power. With the JFS running, power is available to operate the AMAD fire warning system, the intercom system between pilot and the ground, and the cockpit utility light. Engine RPM and FTIT gages are inoperative until the emergency generator comes on line during start. The rest of the engine instruments are inoperative until a main generator comes on line at about 44% RPM during the first engine start.

(PW-220) ENG CONTR switch position should not be changed until 60 seconds after start initiation due to the possible failure of the CGB shear section, hot start, start-stall, or torching during start. Switch may be positioned to desired setting once engine achieves idle.

Because a JFS accumulator was discharged to start the JFS, the JFS LOW light will illuminate when power is available to light the caution panel. It will go out when the accumulators are recharged by a running engine.

When the finger lift is raised, the JFS will engage and accelerate the engine. JFS engagement is indicated by an audible decrease in JFS whine when the JFS clutch engages (BMS sounds WIP). A normal start is indicated by RPM acceleration occurring before initial FTIT movement.

Monitor engine instruments and compare against the operating limitations listed in section V. After first engine start, the JFS automatically decouples from that engine and is ready for the second engine start. After second engine start, the JFS shuts down automatically.

If an engine must be shut down and restarted before the JFS low light has extinguished, avoid starting the JFS on a partially charged bottle. Service the JFS via the ground comm menu (T, 7) prior to a second JFS start attempt.
The following procedure is applicable to either engine. The right engine is normally started first to permit checking utility hydraulic pressure with only the right pump operating.

items.text: Failure to ensure all flight control surfaces move to the proper position for each stick movement may result in loss of control. Malfunctions can exist which would cause the flight controls to be correct with stick in one position and incorrect in another position.

Release brakes and advance power slightly if necessary. As aircraft starts to roll, apply brakes to check operation. When clear, actuate nose gear steering in both directions to ensure proper operation. During taxi, check all flight instruments. Due to excess thrust at idle power, taxi speed requires continual attention. At high gross weights, make all turns at minimum practicable speed and maximum practicable radius.

items.note: If the aircraft is manually trimmed nose down from takeoff trim, nosewheel lift-off speed may be increased.
The canopy may bounce slightly as it lowers on canopy sill.

items.text: Advance engines to 80% (some aircraft creep may occur) and check instruments. When ready for takeoff, release brakes and advance throttles to MIL or MAX as desired.
Monitor engine instruments for proper operation, assuring that nozzles remain below 30% at MIL.

For normal takeoffs, move the stick to approximately 10° pitch attitude. For maximum performance takeoffs (minimum ground roll), move the stick full aft at a speed below the nose wheel lift-off speed and rotate 12° pitch attitude.
Retract gear and flaps when airborne.

During normal afterburner operation, observe exhaust nozzles open progressively with each afterburner segment; thrust and fuel flow increase proportionately. As throttles are advanced from minimum to maximum afterburner, the increase in thrust is fairly smooth and continuous.
MIL Power - Climb at 350 knots to 0.90 Mach, then maintain 0.90 MACH.
MAX Power - Climb at 350 knots to 0,95 Mach. If Mach increases above 0,95 at 40° pitch attitude, hold 40° and allow the Mach to increase.
Continually monitor aircraft systems operation throughout the flight. Frequently check engine instruments, cabin pressure, oxygen system operation, fuel quantity and fuel transfer.

Optimal cruise and maximum endurance should be found in the performance data section and is attained by flying the correct Mach number for configuration and altitude. If the performance charts are not available and accuracy is not a significant factor, 12 units AOA may be used for optimum cruise and 14.5 units AOA may be used for maximum endurance.

items.text: ALN Light Not On or Not Flashing (During Alignment)

If the ALN light does not illuminate within approximately 60 seconds, check that the ADI is erect (INS selected on the ADI mode switch), current present position (within 600ft/0.1 arc minutes) is displayed, and the ALN light tests good. If the ADI has not started to erect, the align cycle did not initialize. If the INS is shutdown (NCI mode selector knob in OFF), leave NCI mode selector knob in OFF for a minimum 2 seconds before initiating another alignment. Switching the NCI mode selector knob from NAV to GC or STOR causes the INS to start a new alignment cycle.
Aircraft Movement While in Align Mode

If the aircraft is moved while the INS is in an align mode, the INS auto-transitions to NAV mode and the ALN light stops flashing. After stopping the aircraft, the INU reenters the align mode and the ALN light begins flashing again after approximately 1 minute. As soon as the light begins flashing, the NCI mode selector knob may be placed in the NAV mode. If the alignment is not completed, the INS provides degraded navigational performance and should be restarted by turning the INS off (INS mode selector knob to OFF) for a minimum of 2 seconds, then to GC ALIGN for a full GC alignment. The NCI mode selector knob can then be switched to INS or the INS will automatically transition to Nav (INS) at aircraft takeoff.

Loss of normal brakes may be caused by a defective anti-skid system, faulty brakes, or a UTL A hydraulic pressure loss. Malfunction of the anti-skid system may not illuminate the anti-skid light; however, failures may be recognized by no apparent braking action. In any case, it is important to remember when assessing the status of brakes, that very little deceleration will be sensed by the pilot at speeds above 100 knots regardless of whether the anti-skid system has failed. Therefore, aerodynamic braking should be accomplished first during the landing roll, followed by braking action as required.
If brake failure occurs during landing roll, consider lowering the hook before attempting to restore braking.
If loss of the brakes is determined, turn the anti-skid switch to PULSER at high speed or OFF at taxi speed.
During pulser operation, pedal pressure over that required for safe deceleration may cause excessive tire wear and/or blown tires.

If braking is not restored, pulling the emergency brake/steering handle provides an alternate power source for brakes/steering and bypasses the anti-skid/pulser system. Sufficient accumulator pressure is available to safely stop the aircraft. Repeated brakes applications deplete the system faster than a smooth steady application. If UTL B is operating, the JFS accumulator remains charged. If the JFS LOW light is on, the emergency brake system is not reliable for taxi since the accumulator pressure can no longer be monitored. Do not pull the emergency brake/steering handle in flight as the nosewheel may follow rudder commands, and touchdown steering/wheel brake protection is lost. If UTL A is available, normal operation can be restored by pushing the emergency brake/steering handing and releasing the paddle switch. While taxiing, if stopping distance is critical, use the emergency brake/steering handle first.

Directional control problems with the nose gear on the ground may be caused by a blown tire, nose gear shimmy, defective nose gear steering, defective anti-skid, overextended strut, or a faulty brake. For a known blown tire or brake loss, refer to the appropriate emergency procedure. If the cause of the directional control problem cannot be determined, time spend in fault isolation may worsen the situation. In this case, a single procedure (pulling the emergency brake/steering handle) is recommended. This provides an alternate source for powered braking/steering and disables the anti-skid and pulser system(s), thereby accommodating all of the various failure modes which may have caused the directional control problems. NORMAL/MANEUVERING range steering continues to be available with the emergency brake/steering handle pulled.

If departure from a prepared runway, taxiway or ramp is unavoidable, consider shutting down the engines (time and conditions permitting) to minimize foreign object damage. Directional control while skidding or sliding across an unprepared surface may be impossible. If the aircraft develops a sideways skid or slide, failure of the landing gear is probable due to high side load forces. At higher speeds, aircraft roll, tumble, or groundloop is a possibility and consideration should be given to ground ejection if the situation warrants. Ground egress should not be attempted until the aircraft has come to a stop.

items.note: Because the anti-skid has been disabled, be prepared for a possible wheel lockup and a subsequent blown tire(s).
This ensures that the nose gear steering shifts to JFS hydraulic accumulator pressure.

items.text:
The decision to abort or continue the takeoff depends on many factors, most of which relate to a specific takeoff situation. Considerations should include, but are not limited to, the following:
a. Runway factors: Runway remaining, surface condition (wet, dry, etc.), type and/or number of arresting gear available, obstructions alongside or at the departure end, wind direction and velocity, weather and visibility.
b. Aircraft factors: Weight, stores configuration, nature of the emergency, velocity at decision point, and importance of getting airborne.
c. Stopping factors: Maximum braking, speed brake, hook, jettisoning stores, engine shutdown.
d. Full aft stick: Full aft stick will reduce stopping distance below computed TOLD data (up to 500 feet at max abort speed) by increasing drag and weight on wheels. However, full aft stick must be applied below rotation speed to avoid raising the nose.

Consider aborting after airborne where sufficient runway is available. Normally, with the short takeoff distances of the aircraft, abort is not a problem, but an early decision provides the most favorable circumstances.

items.note: If aborting with a blown tire or if a main tire blows during abort, place the anti-skid switch in PULSER, and use light braking on the good tire.

items.text: After an abort where unusual braking is required, do not shut down engines until adequate firefighting equipment is available. Hot wheels and brakes can provide an ignition source for fuel drained overboard during engine shutdown.
Two means exist to jettison external stores: the emergency jettison button, on the center instrument panel, and the select jettison button, on the ACP.
The emergency jettison button simultaneously jettisons all pylons and fuselage/CFT mounted missiles (N/I).
Do not use emergency jettison on the ground, or with fuseslage/CFT mounted missiles aboard, except as a last resort or in extreme emergency.

sections.title: Engine Failure/Loss of Thrust/Afterburner Failure on Takeoff

items.text: Do Depending on the type of failure and aircraft conditions, MIL power may not be sufficient to continue takeoff or sustain flight at low airspeed. If takeoff is continued use maximum power available in a three point attitude and accelerate to single engine takeoff speed. Once single engine rotation speed is attained, input 1/2 aft stick, and rotate to a 10° attitude. Reducing pitch (if able) and selecting maximum afterburner will allow the aircraft to accelerate.

If engine failure occurs after rotation, it may be necessary to lower the nose to the runway to attain single engine rotation speed. This is especially important at high gross weights and low-density altitudes. If an engine fails immediately after becoming airborne, it may be necessary to allow the aircraft to settle back to the runway until single engine rotation speed is attained. Immediately after becoming airborne, establish near level flight for acceleration prior to climb. Lateral and directional control can be maintained if the aircraft remains above stall speed, but the ability to climb depends upon the aircraft gross weight, configuration, airspeed, altitude and temperature.
Following an AB anomaly on takeoff and TOLD data requires afterburner, consideration should be given to aborting if conditions warrant.

items.action: lower to three-point attitude and accelerate to SETOS

items.text: With an engine failure or significant loss of thrust, if SETOS is not obtained by lowering nose to the runway, sustained flight may not be possible.
Delaying rotation until higher speeds improves single engine climb performance. Consider runway remaining and tire speed limits (nose 200, mains 225).

items.action: retract as soon as practical after takeoff

items.text: Gear retraction increases single engine rate of climb by 300-500FPM.
